title: Cliff Leeman, a Kansas City drummer who went to New York
summary: Hinton begins a survey of drummers; Jones says Cliff Leeman knew Kansas City music but could not transplant it to New York bands.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That's great; that really brings it up to what we're thinking about, '46. I'd just like to ask you a few question, Jo, about some drummers down through - just to see what kinds of things you want to say about some of the drummers, just to sort of reminisce and talk about some of the drummers, and I'd like you to add anything that you
want and mention other drummers that I might not have thought about. We have mentioned Big Sid -

I worked last week with a drummer that I consider a very great drummer and a milestone in jazz history and he knows you very well and loves you dearly, and I'm sure you love him. But I'd like for you just to say something about him. His name is Cliff Leeman. He said he was around Kansas City when you were around there.

Cliff Leeman came from Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers all the way from Portland, Oregon. Cliff Leeman quit the band in Kansas City and he was a sub-drummer with the jump-up band that Basie had. Nobody ever heard that band to speak of but people like - when Woody Herman came in with Isham Jones, Jerry Jerome was playing across the street but Cliff Leeman was in the place before I'd get there because I was babysitting.
Jerry Jerome was playing right across the street from the Reno, directly across the street. He heard that band; he knew that band.

Cliff without a doubt, with what Cliff knew and how Cliff was playing prior to coming to New York, he was all right. Artie Shaw attempted to change him; and I remember that I was taking Cliff home one night and he lived
up in the Bronx area somewhere. He was awfully ill and the train came and I had to grab Cliff. Cliff was out of commission for about a year.
He's well now and he's doing just fine.

Cliff knew the key and it was very difficult for him, having been in Kansas City and been around people, because he hung out with people - he hung out with Pete Johnson, he hung out with the Lester Youngs, he hung out with the Herschels, he hung out with Hot Lips Page - now for him to come from the other side of the tracks, to come to Easterners here to New York/and try to show them how music go, that's how you get Cliff. Because he knew how it was supposed to go but he could not transplant this thing to these peoples, you see.
